explanations.answer: To keep a vow he had made
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Acts 18:18 says he had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made. The text doesn't tell us what the vow was, so I'm not going to guess. I'll just say a man who keeps his word is a man I'd trust with my dough.

explanations.answer: To mark his last day in Corinth
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since he is leaving Corinth. But the text gives a different reason. Acts 18:18 says he had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made. Cenchrea is on the way out, and the haircut is about the vow.

explanations.answer: To get ready for the long voyage
explanations.explanation: I get it, friend. A long trip, so you tidy up first. But the text doesn't say that. Acts 18:18 says he had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made, then he sailed for Syria. The vow is the reason, and the sailing comes after.
Yes, baker. Acts 18:19 says Paul went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. He doesn't sit back and let the room run itself. He gets right in there and talks it through with them.
Nope, friend. Quiet isn't what Acts 18:19 shows. It says Paul went into the synagogue there and reasoned with the Jews. That's a man talking and making his case, not a man hiding behind a bulletin.

Close to the right building, wrong spot in it. Paul was in the synagogue, but Acts 18:19 says he reasoned with the Jews. He wasn't off in a corner by himself. He was in the middle of the conversation.

I see why you'd say that, baker. They asked him nicely. But Acts 18:20 says that when they asked him to stay for a while longer, he declined. So the answer is False. He said no, and the very next verse gives them a promise.

Right, baker. They asked, and Acts 18:20 says he declined. The text doesn't give a reason, so I won't make one up. But he doesn't leave empty-handed, because he tells them he'll come back if God is willing (Acts 18:21).
That's the one, friend. Paul says, “I will come back to you if God is willing.” (Acts 18:21) He makes the promise and leaves the schedule in God's hands. I've learned that's a good place to leave it.

explanations.answer: If the synagogue writes to him
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but no letter is in this verse. Paul says, “I will come back to you if God is willing.” (Acts 18:21) The condition is God's willingness. Nobody has to send him a thing.

explanations.answer: If the winds turn his way
explanations.explanation: He's about to set sail, so I see why you went there. But the verse never mentions wind. Paul says, “I will come back to you if God is willing.” (Acts 18:21) The condition is God being willing, and that's all he names.
Yes, baker. Acts 18:22 says that after landing at Caesarea, Paul went up and greeted the church at Jerusalem. Then he went down to Antioch. Up, then down. That's a lot of stairs for one man.

Rome is a big name, so it's easy to grab. But it's not in this passage. Acts 18:22 says Paul landed at Caesarea, went up, and greeted the church at Jerusalem. That's where this stop on his trip leads.
Corinth is where Paul just came from, friend. He stayed there for quite some time (Acts 18:18). Now he's moved on. After landing at Caesarea, he greets the church at Jerusalem (Acts 18:22).

That's right, baker. Acts 18:23 says he traveled from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. Galatia and Phrygia are regions, so that's a whole lot of roads. All the disciples, too. He doesn't skip anybody.

Counting would take a clipboard, friend. But Acts 18:23 doesn't say anything about numbers. It says he went from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. He was building them up.

That's a reasonable guess for a traveling teacher. But the text doesn't say it. Acts 18:23 says Paul went through Galatia and Phrygia strengthening all the disciples. Strengthening is the job, and the verse gives it to him.

Yes, baker. Acts 18:24 calls Apollos, a native of Alexandria, an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures. Eloquent means he could really speak. I can barely get through a recipe without losing my place!
Not this time, friend. Acts 18:24 says Apollos was an eloquent man, well versed in the Scriptures. So the answer is True. This man could speak well, and he knew his Scripture.

You got it, baker. Acts 18:25 says he taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. That's the one gap the verse names. The verse still calls him instructed in the way of the Lord and fervent in spirit.
Peter is a famous name, so I see the pull. But Acts 18:25 says Apollos knew only the baptism of John. John is the name the verse gives. Peter isn't in it.
Philip is a name from the book of Acts, but he isn't in this verse. Acts 18:25 says Apollos knew only the baptism of John. That's the missing piece the text names.

explanations.answer: Take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Acts 18:26 says Priscilla and Aquila took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. They pulled him aside, which is the gentle way to do it. If someone ever needs to fix my cookie recipe, I'd pick that way too.

explanations.answer: Correct him right there in front of the whole synagogue
explanations.explanation: Ouch, friend. Picture someone fixing you in front of a whole crowd. That's not what happened. Acts 18:26 says they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. They did it privately.

explanations.answer: Tell him to stop teaching until Paul comes back
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says they told him to stop. Acts 18:26 says they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. They taught him more, and Paul isn't part of that scene.

I get why you'd think so, since friends can be nervous about a goodbye. But Acts 18:27 says the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. So the answer is False. They cheered him on and sent a letter ahead.
Right, baker. Acts 18:27 says the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples in Achaia to welcome him. They didn't hold him back. They backed him up and sent a letter ahead.

That's right, baker. Acts 18:28 says he powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. Remember, he was well versed in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). Same strength, now with a fuller understanding of the way of God.

Signs and wonders show up elsewhere in Acts, so it's an easy one to pick. But not here. Acts 18:28 says he was proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. The Scriptures are the tool this verse names.

That sounds exciting, friend, but the verse doesn't mention visions. Acts 18:28 says he powerfully refuted the Jews in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ. He used the Scriptures, and he used them in public.
